# Running tests

**track**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs about 1,800 tests in four tracks at once, in about 9 to 11 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 500 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in under a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`) or the parser, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

Three limits of `ledger.py` (below):

- A row at its 1,200-character limit takes no further note.
- No command edits a row's claim. `close --claim` takes a corrected one.
- Its heading reader does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.

# Climb batch 16, rung S (rung-solver-speed): the checker's solver reduces once, and a guard on the build's long methods

- problem: after the walker split about 95 % of the component's typeCheck was the solver, `Formula.reduce` 94.8 % and `normConjunct`'s pair test 94.9 % inclusive (`explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md`, section 2.3); measured here, 35.1M reductions over the component, 34.4M of formulas already reduced (section 4), at `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:356` and `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:721` (528438ac5)
- spec: the specification names no time of the checker: `grep -rliE 'memoi|checker.{0,40}(time|speed|fast)' Specification/basic Specification/basic-lib` prints nothing; none
- precedent: row 688's ground memo and the normalize memos' context marks, at 528438ac5 `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala:104-115` and `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:569-573`
- deviation: the reduction memo lives on the analyzer, keyed by the formula alone, where the ground memo lives on the table keyed by the question and the negation: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:589-609`
- deviation: the exclusion memo keys a question with its inference variables renamed apart, which no memo of the tree did before: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:985-1015`
- deviation: the exclusion answers that read no context are shared through the table as Booleans, where the ground memo shares formulas: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala:150-156`
- historical: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:358`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:408`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala:34`

## 1. What changed and why

Commits on `wip/rung-solver-speed`, cut from `528438ac5`:

| commit | what |
|---|---|
| `aaac79b84` | tests: `ReductionMemoJUTest` (red on the base) and the guard `MethodSizeJUTest` |
| `615ecff76` | the change: `Formula.reduce` asks the analyzer for a reduction it made before (`TypeAnalyzer.reduced`) |
| `60d8081ea` | tests: `ExclusionMemoJUTest` and `TraitTableMemoJUTest` (red on the change) |
| `6e6192747` | the second pass: the exclusion memo by renamed question, and the table's two lookups |

**The change.** `Formula.reduce` simplifies a conjunction or a disjunction. For each inference variable it meets the upper bounds and joins the lower bounds, then tests them for contradiction and redundancy, each test a subtype or exclusion question (`Formula.scala:365-466`).

- `Formula.and` and `or` reduce after every step of their fold. `implies`, `isTrue`, `isFalse` and `equivalent` reduce both sides, and `maximalCFormulas` reduces each pair.
- So the same formula is reduced again and again: 35,107,747 reductions over the component, 34,447,211 of them of a formula already in reduced form (section 4).

Now `reduce` sends an `And` or an `Or` to `TypeAnalyzer.reduced` (`Formula.scala:360-363`), which keeps each analyzer's answers (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:589-609`):

- **The key is the formula.** A reduction asks only the analyzer's public questions (`meet`, `join`, `subtype`, `excludes`, `lteq`, `definitelyExcludes`), each from an empty cycle history. So its answer depends on the formula and on the analyzer's trait table and kind environment, and the analyzer owns the memo. The negation flag takes no part: no reduction is asked under a negation.
- **Context reads.** An answer whose computation read the context (`traits.contextReads` moved) is marked, and a hit on it is a context read too (`traits.readContext()`). So an enclosing computation is never shared by the ground memo as context-free. This is the normalize memos' rule (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:616-620`).
- **Opened sizes.** A reduction that opened a size (`Formula.openedSizeCount` moved, `Formula.scala:150`) is not kept: computed again, it would open a fresh size with another name.
- **The switch** is `fortress.analyzer.reduce.cache`, default on, beside the analyzer's other switches.

**The second pass.** After the change, the profile held `TypeAnalyzer.dExc` at 62.7 % inclusive, from `normConjunct`'s pair test `x.exists(y => x.exists(z => dExc(y, z)))` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:768`). It also held the trait table's walk of every type it holds: `TraitTable.find` at `pSubInner`'s declaration search 11.9 %, `TraitTable.typeCons` 6.6 % (section 5). The pass takes all three:

- **The exclusion memo.** `dExc` keeps its answers by the question with its type inference variables renamed apart (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:408-439`; `renamedApart`, `:985-1015`).
  - An inference call makes fresh variables, so `Number` against `MultiplicativeRing[\$i\]` was asked with a new `$i` each time and never met a memo.
  - The answer is a Boolean, and it is the same under every renaming of the variables, because the computation compares them only by equality.
  - It is kept only from an empty cycle history and marked if its computation read the context. If it read none, it is shared through the trait table (`TraitTable.scala:150-156`), as the ground memo shares its answers. It is not kept if the computation opened a size.
  - A question that holds a size or operator inference variable is not kept.
  - The renamed variables hash by their number, so a renaming asks the JVM for no identity hash.
  - The switch is `fortress.analyzer.exclusion.cache`.
- **`TraitTable.typeCons`** keeps its answer by the name's api and text (`TraitTable.scala:34-53`). An `Id`'s span takes no part in a lookup, since `SpanInfo.equals` is true of any two spans. The indices' maps of types are built once (`CollectUtil.immutable`, `compiler/index/CompilationUnitIndex.java:41`).
- **The declaration search.** `pSubInner` searched for a trait's declaration by its text, walking every type of the table for every comparison of two instances of one generic trait (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:271` at 528438ac5). It is now `traits.declaredTypeCons(text)` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:267`; `TraitTable.scala:55-66`): the same walk, once per name. The table's walk meets its types in the same order each time, while the table holds the same types.
- Both lookups share the switch `fortress.analyzer.typecons.cache`.

**The guard.** `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/MethodSizeJUTest.java`, in the misc track, reads every class under `ProjectFortress/build` with `java.lang.classfile`, as `WalkerJUTest` reads `Walker` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/WalkerJUTest.java:59-76`).

- It fails on any method over 8,000 bytes of bytecode that its list does not name, and names each such method with its size.
- It also fails on a listed method that is gone from the build or back under the limit, so that the list stays true.
- `WalkerJUTest` is as it was. The list is in section 8.

## 3. Where the fix belongs, and the precedent search

The solver is the compiled checker's own (`explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md`, B.6):

- `Formula.scala` holds the constraint formulas and their reduction.
- `TypeAnalyzer.scala` holds the subtype, exclusion and normal-form questions.
- `TraitTable.scala` is the table that every analyzer over one compilation unit shares.

Walk shares none of this code, so the fix is the checker's, and only the compiled path sees it. No rule of the language moves (section 9).

**The precedent.** The tree has memoized the checker four times, each in `TypeAnalyzer.scala` or `TraitTable.scala`:

- The analyzer's per-question memos, keyed by the question and the whole cycle history: `pSubMemo`, `pExcMemo` and the five normalize memos (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:97`, `:460`, `:611-620`).
- Rung M's clause memos on the table, for `parents` and `excludesClause` (`TraitTable.scala:116-131`; F-65).
- Row 688's ground memo on the table. An answer that read neither the kind environment nor the cycle history, counted by `contextReads`, is shared by every analyzer over the table (`TraitTable.scala:134-148`; `explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md`, section 6).
- The normalize memos' marks: a key whose value read the context is marked, and a hit on it is a context read (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:616-620`).

Sites in these files that repaired the same defect, a question computed again:

- `TraitTable.scala`: three memos at the base (`parentsMemo`, `excludesClauseMemo`, `groundMemo`), six after the pass (adding `typeConsMemo`, `declaredMemo` and `sharedExclusions`).
- `TypeAnalyzer.scala`: seven memos at the base (`pSubMemo`, `pExcMemo` and five normalize memos), nine after (adding `reduceMemo` and `exclusionMemo`).

I followed three precedents:

- the normalize memos' marking rule, for both new analyzer memos;
- the ground memo's sharing rule, for the exclusion answers that read no context;
- the clause memos' form (a `ConcurrentHashMap` on the table, `putIfAbsent`), for the two table lookups.

## 4. The ways weighed, each with its measure

Every measure below is a count-stage run of a copy compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path (`compiler.md`, "Testing an edit here"), on the base build or on this tree's. None is a timed run.

| way | what it measured | taken |

| A memo of normalized meets, shared by the analyzers over one table (the probe's first way) | probe 1, base: 286,255 intersections normalized, 232,142 of them memo hits and 54,113 computed. Of the 23,832 computed at the outermost level (248.8 s), a shared memo of context-free answers would answer 9,249, worth 0.21 s; 0 mismatches | no: nearly no gain |

The prototypes' times come from one run each on a loaded machine, so they rank the ways and measure nothing finer; section 7 has the timed runs. A second run of the all-on prototype reused its scratch folder's caches, so it skipped the apis' checks; I do not count it. The two prototype variants with the exclusion memo lost `:130` in their outputs, as the final code's distance stage did (section 10).

**The keys, and why each input of an answer is in them:**

- **Reduction**: the formula, on the analyzer. A reduction reads the formula and the analyzer's trait table and kind environment, which are fixed for the analyzer (`class TypeAnalyzer(val traits: TraitTable, val env: KindEnv)`). It reads no cycle history, since each of its questions starts from an empty one, and no negation. The opened-sizes counter is the one global state that a reduction moves, and a reduction that moves it is not kept.
- **Exclusion, in the analyzer**: the two types with their inference variables renamed apart, kept from an empty history only. The answer reads the two types up to renaming, the table and the environment as above, and the history, which is empty. The negation is always off: `exc` asks `pExc` with `negate = false`.
- **Exclusion, shared by the table**: the same key, kept only when the computation read no context, so it read neither the environment nor the history. The table owns the memo.
- **`typeCons`**: the name's api and text, on the table. The answer reads the name's api name and text (the span takes no part) and the table's compilation unit and global environment, which are fixed.
- **The declaration search**: the name's text, on the table. The answer reads the text and the table's set of types, which is fixed. The walk meets the types in one order while the set and its members' identity hashes stay the same.

- **`unmarked-context-reads`** would count an answer marked context-free whose computation read the context. It is 0 for both memos.
- **The change's `text-mismatches`** counts answers that are equal as formulas but whose text differs, a set's members in another order: 116,461 of 7.15M. An equal formula is the same answer, and none of these reached the output (section 7).
- **`:130`**: the change's audited run lost row 488's `:130` (38 / 37). The final code's audits kept it: 39 / 38 on the count stage, 49 on the distance stage, each equal to its landed table.

## 7. The results and the time

**Machine**: nproc 4, Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz, 2100.000 MHz, openjdk 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`.

- The VM restarted at about 11:15 UTC, between the earlier session's base run and this session's, so I timed the base again.
- The machine was not idle in this session. Other trees' JVMs ran throughout: the distance stages of `fortress-probe-power` and `fortress-probe-where`, and rung H's runs.
- I waited the 30 minutes that `compiler.md` asks, from 11:43, and took the pair at 12:14.

| run | tree and code | start (UTC) | load at start | other trees' JVMs | seconds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | `/home/user/fortress-base16`, `528438ac5` | 12:14:21 | 5.60 | 3 | 437 |
| change | this tree, `615ecff76`'s code (built 11:42; `javap` shows `reduced` and no `renamedApart`, `declaredTypeCons`) | 12:21:38 | 6.55 | 3 | 149 |
| pass | this tree, `6e6192747` | 12:27:04 | 3.59 | 1 | 97 |
| base, earlier session | `/home/user/fortress-base16` | 10:04:47 | 0.43 | 0 | 302 |

- **Gain against the base**: the change 66 % (437 s to 149 s), the pass 78 % (437 s to 97 s). Both are far past the 6 % by which two idle runs of one tree differ. The pass against the change is 35 % faster, but its load at start was lighter, so part of that is the load.
- **For scale**: the count stage took 325 s at climb batch 15b's gate, and 333 s and 352 s idle in the probe.

**Results.** The base and change runs: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh tmp/count/base2.txt tmp/count/base2` from the base build, and the same with `change` from this tree. The pass ran in the brief's post-edit form (`checker-count-postedit.txt`, `cc-post`).

    diff tmp/count/base2.txt tmp/count/change.txt                                  (prints nothing)
    diff tmp/count/base2.txt tmp/rung-solver-speed/checker-count-postedit.txt      (prints nothing)
    diff tmp/count/base2.txt explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-15b/gate/checker-count.txt   (prints nothing)
    diff <(sed 's|/home/user/fortress-base16|TREE|g' tmp/count/base2/run.txt) <(sed 's|/home/user/fortress-solverspeed|TREE|g' tmp/count/change/run.txt)   (prints nothing)
    diff <(sed 's|/home/user/fortress-solverspeed|TREE|g' tmp/count/change/run.txt) <(sed 's|/home/user/fortress-solverspeed|TREE|g' tmp/rung-solver-speed/cc-post/run.txt)   (prints nothing)

- The three tables are equal: `#total 39`, `#locations 38`, every api 0, `#crash none`.
- The three whole outputs are equal once the tree path is masked, 178 lines each, with no line in another order.
- Row 488's `:130` stays in all three.

## 8. The guard's list

I scanned the base build with `tmp/rung-solver-speed/scan/Scan.java` over `/home/user/fortress-base16/ProjectFortress/build` (4,117 classes). It found twelve methods over 8,000 bytes, and the list is those twelve, each with what runs it (`MethodSizeJUTest.java:32-52`):

| method | bytes | what runs it |
|---|---|---|
| `com.sun.fortress.nodes.NodeReader.readNode` | 14,026 | each read of a syntax tree from a cache entry (`nodes_util/FortressNodeReader.java:32`) |
| `com.sun.fortress.parser.Fortress.pCharLiteralContent$1` | 23,717 | the parser, at each character literal |
| `com.sun.fortress.parser.preparser.PreFortress.pCharLiteralContent$1` | 23,717 | the preparser, the same |
| `com.sun.fortress.parser.templateparser.TemplateParser.pCharLiteralContent$1` | 23,717 | the template parser, the same |
| `com.sun.fortress.scala_src.disambiguator.ExprDisambiguator.walk` | 8,518 | the disambiguator, on both paths |
| `com.sun.fortress.scala_src.typechecker.impls.Misc.checkExprMisc` | 12,893 | the compiled checker, at each expression that `Dispatch` sends it (`impls/Dispatch.scala:98`) |
| `com.sun.fortress.scala_src.linker.HygienicRenamer.walk` | 11,599 | nothing in the tree constructs a `HygienicRenamer` |
| `com.sun.fortress.useful.MagicNumbers.<clinit>` | 16,677 | the class's initializer, once |
| `com.sun.fortress.numerics.DirectedRoundingTestData.make_double_divide_data` | 21,975 | the data of `DirectedRoundingTest`'s `main`, which no suite runs |
| `...DirectedRoundingTestData.make_double_multiply_data` | 10,229 | the same |
| `...DirectedRoundingTestData.make_float_divide_data` | 10,425 | the same |
| `...DirectedRoundingTestData.make_float_multiply_data` | 9,715 | the same |

- The probe and its skeptic named the first seven (`checker-speed-2/REPORT.md` section 2.2, `SKEPTIC.md` section 5). The scan adds `MagicNumbers.<clinit>` and the four `DirectedRoundingTestData` methods.
- The skeptic's `pidrest`, 7,617 bytes, is under the limit, so it is not listed.
- The guard keys a method by its class and name, and takes the largest size among its overloads.

## 9. What the specification settles, and the sentences made false

The specification does not speak of the checker's time (the grep in the provenance lines), and no rule moves: the checker accepts and refuses the same programs, with the same errors at the same places (section 7). So the change makes no sentence of the specification false, no Appendix I Effect and no note on walk or the compiled path.

Sentences of the skill that the change makes false, for the gather and the skill writer:

- `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/compiler.md:125`: "The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 6 minutes on an idle machine." It took 97 s on this rung's final code at load 3.6, and the distance stage took 574 s (section 10).
- `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/compiler.md:134` names `WalkerJUTest` as the one guard of a long method. `MethodSizeJUTest` now guards every method of the build.
- The batch brief's "the count (about 5 minutes, 280 to 390 s in climb batches 13b and 14)", and "the distance (about half an hour, one core: 26 to 29 minutes in climb batch 14)".
- F-231's "What remains is about 95 % the solver normalizing meets again" is now wrong (record.md).

## 10. The count, the distance and the ladder

The rung edits `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/`, which is outside the paths where neither stage can move. So both stages ran once on the final code (`6e6192747`).

**Count**: see section 7. Its table equals climb batch 15b's gate table (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-15b/gate/checker-count.txt`), and the count stays 39.

**Distance**:

    explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh tmp/rung-solver-speed/distance-postedit.txt tmp/rung-solver-speed/dist-post
        #total	48
        #seconds	574	FortressLibrary 474
        #machine	nproc=4; Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz; 2100.000 MHz; load at start 4.58 5.29 5.32; openjdk version "25.0.4.1" 2026-08-18; FORTRESS_THREADS=1
    explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-15b/gate/distance.txt tmp/rung-solver-speed/distance-postedit.txt
        DISTANCE DOWN   49 -> 48 (-1)
            kind typecheck               40 -> 39     (-1)
            class BR                      4 -> 3      (-1)  big operators: a reduction's body typed as the element, not the BigReduction or Comprehension declared
            unit component FortressLibrary     43 -> 42     (-1)

Site by site, I compared `tmp/rung-solver-speed/dist-post/errors.tsv` with `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, both sorted. The rung edits no library line, so lines map one to one and row 577 does not apply. One row is gone, none is added and none respelled:

    < typecheck	Function body has type TotalComparison, but declared return type is BigReduction[\..\].	-	component FortressLibrary	typecheck	FortressLibrary.fss:130	Function body has type TotalComparison, but declared return type is BigReduction[\TotalComparison,TotalComparison\].

This is row 488's `:130`, the `BIG LEXICO` at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:129-130`. The audit beside it:

- The audit copy of the same final code, run as the distance stage (section 6), reuses 428M answers with 0 differences.
- Its table reads `DISTANCE SAME   49`, and its `errors.tsv` equals the landed per-site list row for row, `:130` included.
- So the run that computes every reused answer again keeps `:130`, every reuse gives the answer computed again, and the run that does not compute them again loses `:130`.

This is F-232's move: row 488's site depends on what the checker queried earlier. It is not a result that the change made. The count stage keeps `:130` in base, change and pass. The merged tree's distance may read 48 or 49 by the same mechanism.

**Ladder subset**: I copied the drivers of `gate.md`, "The ladder regression", into `tmp/rung-solver-speed/ladder/`. The subset is 68 files (decision 11) plus the eighteen microGPT components, run after the pass was built.

- 61 of the 68 have the phase and first error of the baseline's `raw/` (2026-09-19).
- 7 moved since the baseline:
  - `FailInference2` typecheck → pass;
  - `expTest` → disambiguate;
  - `overloadTest6` → codegen;
  - `restTest`, `restTest2` and `restTest2a`: another first error, about a varargs type;
  - `simpleExp`: another first error, an ambiguous coercion.
- I compiled each of the 7 on the base's code (`/home/user/fortress-base16/explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base16 tmp/old-caches compile tests/X.fss`). Each output equals the new one, line for line, except `Operation took`. These are the base's own moves, from landings since the baseline; none comes from this rung.
- microGPT: `diff <(mg_phases explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-15b/gate/ladder/microgpt-phase.md) <(mg_phases tmp/rung-solver-speed/ladder/microgpt-phase.md)` prints nothing. Every component stops at disambiguate, before the checker.

## 11. Old against new

- The count stage over the interpreter's library: base build against this tree, three timed runs, tables and outputs equal (section 7).
- The distance stage against the landed per-site list, and its audit copy (section 10).
- The 7 ladder files that moved since the baseline, each compiled on the base's code (section 10).
- Walk shares none of the edited code, so I ran no walk program.

## 12. Points to report

- **Each count run's seconds and load at start, and the gain against the base**: base 437 s at 5.60, change 149 s at 6.55, pass 97 s at 3.59; gains 66 % and 78 % (section 7).
- **The way taken and the ways weighed, each with its measure; the memo's key and why every input of its answer is in it**: section 4.
- **The audit**: on the count stage, 7,147,587 reductions, 153,930 exclusions, 156,462,352 type lookups and 183,577 declaration searches reused, 0 differences. On the distance stage, 428M reuses, 0 differences (section 6).
- **Any difference in a table or a whole output, each line named; a move of row 488's `:130`, with the audit beside it**:
  - None in the count stage: `:130` stays in base, change and pass.
  - The final code's distance stage lost `:130`, the one line named in section 10. The audit copy of the same code kept it, with 0 differences.
  - Two instrumented runs also lost `:130`: the change's count-stage audit and the base's JFR run.
  - This is F-232's move.
- **The guard's allow-list, each method with its size and what runs it**: section 8.
- **A checker file edited beyond the three named, or any library, walk or AST edit**: none. The rung edits `Formula.scala`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala` and `TraitTable.scala`, and adds four test files.

## 13. Decisions

1. **The change is a memo of each analyzer's reductions**, not a reordered fold, a shared memo of meets or a shared memo of reductions.
   - A reordered fold changes the formulas it carries, so it can change answers.
   - A shared memo of normalized meets would save 0.21 s.
   - A reduction memo shared across analyzers adds 3,658 hits to 34.56M.
   - Evidence: section 4, probes 1 and 3.
   - No decision of the curator covers the choice among these. P-148 and the coordinator's call on Q2 ask for a pass that changes no result.
2. **The second pass takes the exclusion memo by renamed question, in the analyzer and shared through the table, and the table's two lookups.** It does not take the `maximalCFormulas` rewrite (no gain, section 4) or a halving of the pair test (answers could move). Evidence: the change's JFR (section 5) and the prototypes (section 4).
3. **The exclusion memo renames inference variables apart**, a reuse that the tree had not made before.
   - Ways not taken: keying by the exact question (probe 5: 7.1 s of the 35.8 s), and keying by the environment's text, which is not a faithful key.
   - Evidence: probe 5; the audits' 153,930 and 400,171 exclusion reuses with 0 differences; and the argument in section 4 that the Boolean answer compares variables only by equality.
4. **The exclusion memo keeps answers only from an empty cycle history.** A renaming of a non-empty history would follow the history set's iteration order, which follows identity hashes. Way not taken: keying by the renamed history.

new='''class TraitTable(current: CompilationUnitIndex, globalEnv: GlobalEnvironment) extends Iterable[TypeConsIndex] {
  // Memos for typeCons and declaredTypeCons, sound while both depend on nothing but this table and
  // the name (its api and its text; a span takes no part in a lookup): the indices' maps of types
  // do not change once built.
  private final val cacheTypeCons = ProjectProperties.getBoolean("fortress.analyzer.typecons.cache", true)
  private val typeConsMemo = new ConcurrentHashMap[(Option[APIName], String), JOption[TypeConsIndex]]()
  private val declaredMemo = new ConcurrentHashMap[String, Option[TypeConsIndex]]()

  def typeCons(name: Id): JOption[TypeConsIndex] =
    if (!cacheTypeCons) lookUpTypeCons(name)
    else {
      val key = (if (name.getApiName.isSome) Some(name.getApiName.unwrap) else None, name.getText)
      typeConsMemo.get(key) match {
        case null =>
          val result = lookUpTypeCons(name)
          val raced = typeConsMemo.putIfAbsent(key, result)
          if (raced == null) result else raced
        case v => v
      }
    }

  /** The first type of this table, in its walk, that declares a trait or object of the given name. */
  def declaredTypeCons(text: String): Option[TypeConsIndex] =
    if (!cacheTypeCons) findDeclared(text)
    else declaredMemo.get(text) match {
      case null =>
        val result = findDeclared(text)
        val raced = declaredMemo.putIfAbsent(text, result)
        if (raced == null) result else raced
      case v => v
    }

#!/bin/bash
# the count stage timed on the base build, then on this tree's build (the change), one after the other
W=/home/user/fortress-solverspeed
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$W/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$W/tmp"
for run in base2 change; do
  if [ $run = base2 ]; then cd /home/user/fortress-base16; else cd $W; fi
  export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD
  { date -u; uptime; git rev-parse HEAD; ps -eo pid,etimes,pcpu,args | grep '[j]ava' | cut -c1-160; for p in $(pgrep java); do echo "$p $(readlink /proc/$p/cwd)"; done; } > $W/tmp/count/$run.load
  s=$(date +%s)
  explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$run.txt $W/tmp/count/$run > $W/tmp/count/$run.log 2>&1
  rc=$?
  echo "seconds $(( $(date +%s) - s )) rc=$rc" >> $W/tmp/count/$run.log
done

(* Skeptic's differential program: generic overloads told apart by excluding bounds, and generic methods inferred at many calls. *)
component SkSolverGen
export Executable

trait Aa end
trait Bb excludes { Aa } end
trait Cc end
object A extends Aa end
object B extends Bb end
object C extends { Aa, Cc } end
object D extends { Bb, Cc } end

f[\T extends Aa\](x: T): String = "fA"
f[\T extends Bb\](x: T): String = "fB"

trait Mm[\T\]
    get(): T
end
object MkM[\T\](v: T) extends Mm[\T\]
    get(): T = v
end
wrap[\T\](x: T): Mm[\T\] = MkM[\T\](x)
unwrap[\T\](m: Mm[\T\]): T = m.get()

sel[\T extends Aa\](m: Mm[\T\]): String = "selA"
sel[\T extends Bb\](m: Mm[\T\]): String = "selB"

run(): () = do
    assert(f(A), "fA", "f(A)")
    assert(f(B), "fB", "f(B)")
    assert(f(C), "fA", "f(C)")
    assert(f(D), "fB", "f(D)")
    assert(f(unwrap(wrap(A))), "fA", "f(unwrap(wrap(A)))")
    assert(f(unwrap(wrap(D))), "fB", "f(unwrap(wrap(D)))")
    assert(sel(wrap(A)), "selA", "sel(wrap(A))")
    assert(sel(wrap(B)), "selB", "sel(wrap(B))")
    assert(sel(wrap(C)), "selA", "sel(wrap(C))")
    assert(sel(wrap(D)), "selB", "sel(wrap(D))")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 6 minutes on an idle machine. It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `WalkerJUTest` fails if a method of `Walker` grows past the limit: run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=WalkerJUTest`. If it fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`.

content.content:
#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage's comparison: this table (run.sh's) against the last landed one.
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh <last-landed-table|""> <this-table>
#
# Prints one verdict line, then every #kind and #class row whose count moved, with the
# change, and every #crash row that went or came. It is REPORTED and never red: it always
# exits 0, whatever moved, a stale shadow and a run that produced no table included (Pavol,
# answer 11, POSITIONS.md 2026-09-26: a report-only stage, whose job is driving the distance
# down). The verdicts:
#   DISTANCE DOWN|UP|SAME   <last> -> <now>
#   DISTANCE FIRST          no landed table to compare with
#   DISTANCE NO TABLE       this run produced no count, with the table's own reason
#   SETTING CHANGED         the two tables ran different settings: the counts are not like for like
#   SHADOW STALE            a shadow edit no longer matches the tracked sources
# A move of 2 to 4 errors in the components' type errors or in which pair of LEXICO, SQCAP or
# INVERSE declarations an overloading error names is the checker's run-to-run variation
# (switch-over-distance-flat.md section 5), not a change; a crash row whose line numbers
# moved because a rung edited above it prints as one gone and one new.
set -u
OLD=${1:-}; NEW=${2:?usage: compare.sh <last-landed-table> <this-table>}
field () { awk -F'\t' -v t="$1" '$1 == t { sub("^[^\t]*\t", ""); print; exit }' "$2" ; }

now=$(field '#total' "$NEW")
sh=$(field '#shadow' "$NEW")
case "$sh" in STALE*) echo "SHADOW STALE   ${sh#STALE: }" ;; esac
case "$now" in
  ''|none*) echo "DISTANCE NO TABLE   ${now:-no #total row}" ; exit 0 ;;
esac
if [ -z "$OLD" ] || [ ! -f "$OLD" ] ; then
    echo "DISTANCE FIRST   $now distinct errors, $(field '#distance' "$NEW" | cut -d';' -f1); no landed table to compare with"
    exit 0
fi
was=$(field '#total' "$OLD")
ws=$(field '#distance' "$OLD" | cut -d';' -f1); ns=$(field '#distance' "$NEW" | cut -d';' -f1)
[ "$ws" = "$ns" ] || echo "SETTING CHANGED   was $ws, now $ns: the counts below are not like for like"
case "$was" in ''|none*) echo "DISTANCE $now, the landed table has no count (${was:-no #total row})" ; exit 0 ;; esac
if   [ "$now" -lt "$was" ] ; then echo "DISTANCE DOWN   $was -> $now ($((now - was)))"
elif [ "$now" -gt "$was" ] ; then echo "DISTANCE UP   $was -> $now (+$((now - was)))"
else echo "DISTANCE SAME   $now" ; fi

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
